notes: Case stated appeal on assaulting police constable; Laws LJ upheld magistrates on execution of duty.

enrichment.short_title: Clements: assaulting police constable at Iraq protest march
key_facts: The appellant took part in an anti-Iraq war march near Menwith Hill RAF base and left the prescribed route with a group approaching the perimeter fence.
Police Sergeant Pollard pulled the appellant back by his rucksack after he refused to return to the road; during the struggle the appellant deliberately knocked off the sergeant's helmet.
The magistrates convicted of assaulting a police constable in the execution of his duty but acquitted of resisting arrest.
The appellant argued PS Pollard lacked reasonable grounds to believe the appellant might damage the fence and was therefore not acting in execution of his duty.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Harrogate Magistrates' Court against conviction for assaulting a police constable in the execution of his duty.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the magistrates were entitled to find PS Pollard acted reasonably and in execution of his duty and that knocking off the helmet constituted assault.
enrichment.ratio: An officer intervening during a deliberate departure from a prescribed protest route towards a secure perimeter may reasonably apprehend damage and act in execution of duty; findings within the range open on the evidence will not be disturbed on case stated appeal.
legal_issues: Whether PS Pollard was acting in the execution of his duty when he pulled the appellant back
Whether there was evidence supporting a reasonable apprehension of damage to the fence
Whether rejection of self-defence and defence of another was open to the magistrates
Whether the magistrates' fact findings were supported by the evidence

notes: MHRT conditional discharge JR; tribunal decision quashed for inadequate reasons rejecting one-way medical evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Home Secretary v MHRT: conditional discharge of restricted patient quashed
key_facts: The patient was convicted of violent offences against neighbours arising from longstanding paranoid delusions and detained under sections 37 and 41.
The Mental Health Review Tribunal conditionally discharged her subject to medication and community supervision, deferring discharge until arrangements were made.
The RMO Dr Kehoe and nursing staff gave unanimous evidence that she would not comply with medication if discharged and posed significant risk, especially to former victims.
The Tribunal preferred the patient's undertaking to take medication and found only one prior violent episode, but gave inadequate reasons for rejecting the medical evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review by the Home Secretary of a Mental Health Review Tribunal decision granting conditional discharge of a restricted patient.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; the Tribunal decision was quashed and the matter remitted to a fresh tribunal for inadequate reasons, especially as to medication compliance and risk.
enrichment.ratio: Where medical evidence on medication compliance and risk is one way, a tribunal must explain why it rejects the RMO's evidence and cannot rely on undisclosed reasons; following H and Ashworth, preference for the patient's evidence without adequate explanation vitiates the decision.
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal erred in conflating nature and degree under the Mental Health Act 1983
Whether adequate reasons were given for rejecting unanimous medical evidence on medication compliance
Whether risk assessments in hospital were wrongly treated as applying in the community
Application of Article 5 ECHR and the H and Ashworth reasons challenge
linked_authorities: R (H) v Mental Health Review Tribunal, North and East London Region [2002] EWCA Civ 923
R v London South and South West Region Mental Health Review Tribunal, ex parte Moyle

confidence.notes: Detailed medical evidence, reasons inadequacy finding and quashing order are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Part 1 EAW appeal; warrant lacked conduct particulars capable of constituting extradition offences.

enrichment.short_title: Palar v Belgium: defective European Arrest Warrant for credit card fraud
key_facts: Belgium issued a Part 1 European Arrest Warrant against Gheorghe Palar for IT swindle, forgery and criminal association.
The warrant described cloned Tesco-Club card data linked to cards issued to the appellant and telephone conversations between co-suspects, largely in subjunctive terms.
A Bow Street district judge ordered extradition, holding he need only be satisfied the specified offences were extradition offences.
The appellant appealed on the sole ground that the warrant failed to specify conduct capable of constituting the alleged offences.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court under section 26 Extradition Act 2003 against an extradition order following a Part 1 European Arrest Warrant from Belgium.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; extradition order quashed and appellant discharged because no conduct reasonably capable of constituting the extradition offences was described in the warrant.
enrichment.ratio: A Part 1 warrant must contain particulars of the conduct alleged to constitute the offence under section 2(4)(c); co-operative comity cannot supply missing conduct against the named person, and third parties' acts or vague inferences from telephone calls are insufficient.
legal_issues: Whether the Belgian warrant contained sufficient particulars of conduct under section 2(4)(c)
Whether conduct of third parties could satisfy the extradition offence test
Whether the warrant could itself serve as a section 64(2) certificate
Application of Castillo on fair and accurate description of alleged conduct
linked_authorities: Castillo v Kingdom of Spain [2004] EWHC 1676 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Statutory scheme, warrant contents and allowance of appeal are clearly and fully explained.

notes: SENDISTAT appeal on school exclusions; fixed-term exclusions held justified and reasonable adjustments made.

enrichment.short_title: R v OL Primary School: disability discrimination and fixed-term exclusions

statutes_considered.title: Special Educational Needs and Disability Act 2001

key_facts: R, an eight-year-old pupil with global developmental delay and behavioural difficulties, received ten fixed-term exclusions totalling 38 days for violence and disruption.
The SENDISTAT found less favourable treatment but held exclusions justified on health, safety and discipline grounds and that reasonable adjustments had been made.
The school provided full-time learning support and expert advice but could not place R in the small group recommended for a mainstream primary.
Parents appealed on points of law contending the tribunal should have considered reasonable adjustments before justification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 11 Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 from a SENDISTAT decision dismissing a disability discrimination claim against a primary school.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on all five grounds; fixed-term exclusions were materially and substantially justified and the school had made reasonable adjustments.
enrichment.ratio: Less favourable treatment by exclusion may be justified where material and substantial reasons exist and reasonable adjustments have been made; tribunals need not consider the adjustments duty before justification where both hurdles were properly addressed and no breach of the adjustments duty was found.
legal_issues: Whether fixed-term exclusions amounted to unjustified less favourable treatment under Part IV DDA
Whether the tribunal erred in sequence by addressing justification before reasonable adjustments
Whether further reasonable adjustments were required in a mainstream school
Whether health and safety exclusions were limited to medical reasons under DfES guidance
index_terms: Collins v Royal National Theatre Board
linked_authorities: Collins v Royal National Theatre Board [2004] EWCA Civ 144
Mid-Staffordshire General Hospitals NHS Trust v Cambridge [2003] IRLR 556

notes: Parental leave default provisions; minimum one-week blocks upheld using Pepper v Hart.

enrichment.short_title: Rodway v South Central Trains: minimum blocks of parental leave

statutes_considered.title: Maternity and Parental Leave etc Regulations 1999

key_facts: Mr Rodway, a train guard, sought one day's unpaid parental leave on 26 July 2003 to care for his two-year-old son.
South Central Trains refused because the job could not be covered and later disciplined him for unauthorised absence.
Under Schedule 2 default provisions, parental leave could not be taken in periods other than a week or multiples except for disabled children.
The employment tribunal allowed his section 47C claim but the EAT reversed, holding minimum leave was one week.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on construction of Schedule 2 paragraph 7 Maternity and Parental Leave etc Regulations 1999.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; under default provisions an employee may not take parental leave in a period shorter than one week's leave, with costs summarily assessed at £12,000.
enrichment.ratio: Schedule 2 paragraph 7 fixes minimum periods of one week's leave under regulation 14; regulation 14(4) governs aggregation where parties agree shorter periods but does not override the default minimum, as confirmed by ministerial statements under Pepper v Hart.
legal_issues: Whether default parental leave must be taken in blocks of one week
Construction of 'in a period' in Schedule 2 paragraph 7
Relevance of Council Directive 96/34 and framework agreement recitals
Whether regulation 14(4) permits single-day leave under default provisions

confidence.notes: Regulatory text, Hansard material and dismissal with costs are clearly reasoned.

notes: Late IAT permission JR for orphaned Kosovo nephew; exceptional Article 8 case remitted after Huang.

enrichment.short_title: Lekstaka: exceptional Article 8 removal of orphaned Kosovo nephew
key_facts: The claimant, an ethnic Albanian from Kosovo, entered the UK clandestinely aged 16 and lived with his aunt and uncle who treated him as a son after his father was killed and mother disappeared.
Asylum was refused but the adjudicator found family life yet held removal to Kosovo proportionate; the IAT refused permission to appeal.
He had no remaining family in Kosovo or Macedonia and would not qualify under Immigration Rules or the 2003 family concession as a nephew rather than a son.
The claim was brought late after awaiting Huang but Collins J found real prospect of success on exceptional Article 8 grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an Immigration Appeal Tribunal refusal of permission to appeal an adjudicator's dismissal of an Article 8 claim, with delay and Anufrijeva time issues.
enrichment.outcome: IAT refusal quashed and matter remitted; despite Huang's truly exceptional threshold, the claimant's orphaned status and sole family ties in the UK made the case arguably exceptional.
enrichment.ratio: Following Huang, removal may succeed outside the Rules only in truly exceptional cases, but an orphaned minor brought to join refugee relatives, treated as a son yet failing the letter of the Rules, may fall within that narrow class warranting fresh tribunal consideration.
legal_issues: Whether delay barred the judicial review claim
Application of Huang and Razgar truly exceptional test to family life with uncle and aunt
Whether the adjudicator's proportionality analysis was adequate
Relevance of prior policies on dependants and family reunion for refugees
linked_authorities: Huang v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2005] EWCA Civ 105
R (Razgar) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 27
R (Anufrijeva) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] 1 AC 604

confidence.notes: Fact background and Huang-based remittal are detailed though permission to appeal was refused.

notes: Procedural adjournment only; Mummery LJ stood over permission to appeal for inter partes hearing.

enrichment.short_title: Abiola v Daniel: adjournment of permission to appeal application
key_facts: Applications for permission to appeal had been made in proceedings between Abiola and Daniel and others.
Only the applicant was represented when the matter came before Mummery LJ.
The court had skeleton arguments from the respondent which applicant's counsel had not had time to consider.
The judge considered prospects of success relevant to whether to reinstate the permission applications.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory hearing in the Court of Appeal on whether to reinstate applications for permission to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Case stood over for a one-hour inter partes hearing, reserved to Mummery LJ if possible, to decide reinstatement and permission prospects.
enrichment.ratio: Where permission to appeal applications are listed without both sides represented, the court should adjourn for an inter partes hearing and may consider likely prospects of success when deciding whether reinstatement is appropriate.
legal_issues: Whether permission to appeal applications should be reinstated
Appropriate procedure when only one party is represented
Relevance of prospects of success to reinstatement of permission applications

notes: Share purchase retention account construction; GEC's clause 6.2(b) reading upheld on preliminary issue.

enrichment.short_title: GEC v Powell: retention account releases and outstanding warranty claims
key_facts: GEC acquired PII Group Limited for about £310m with £25m held in a retention account to secure warranty and tax covenant claims.
GEC notified claims worth about $141m at the end of the First Claim Period; Independent Counsel adjudicated their value at nil, triggering release of £15m.
GEC then issued proceedings pursuing the claims while warrantors sought declaration that liability was capped at remaining retention funds.
The dispute centred on whether outstanding First Claim Period claims prevented release of the Second Claim Period Maximum Released Amount under clause 6.2(b).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issue trial on construction of clause 6.2(b) of a share purchase agreement governing staged releases from a retention account.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration for GEC; clause 6.2(b) naturally prevents further retention releases at the end of a claim period while earlier-period claims remain undetermined, and words should not be deleted.
enrichment.ratio: Where a share purchase agreement ties staged retention releases to claim periods, clause 6.2(b) expressly blocks release of later tranches if earlier notified claims are unsettled; inconsistent drafting does not justify deleting integral qualifying words absent rectification.
legal_issues: Construction of clause 6.2(b) retention release mechanism
Interaction between Independent Counsel adjudication and subsequent claim periods
Whether qualifying words in clause 6.2 should be deleted as repugnant
Admissibility of pre-contract negotiations for construction or rectification
linked_authorities: Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896
City Alliance Ltd v Oxford Forecasting Services Ltd [2001] 1 All ER (Comm) 233

confidence.notes: Detailed clause analysis and declaration on preliminary issue are clearly reasoned.

notes: Section 51(3) costs against solicitor-director; real party and dishonest conduct upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Goodwood Recoveries v Breen: section 51(3) costs against controlling director
key_facts: Mr Slater's debt recovery company bought a £16,700 guarantee debt from Macloy Ltd's liquidator and pursued Mr Breen despite evidence the debt had been settled in 1999.
Slater was director, shareholder, company secretary and solicitor for the claimant, controlling the litigation even after selling the company for £500.
He deliberately suppressed a key 8 March 1999 letter, lied about instructions to withdraw a bankruptcy petition and sent an improper letter to witness McHale.
The claim failed and the trial judge ordered Slater personally to pay all defendant's costs on an indemnity basis under section 51(3).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a third-party costs order under section 51(3) Supreme Court Act 1981 against the controlling director of an unsuccessful claimant company.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Slater was the real party who caused all the costs and his dishonest conduct justified the exceptional third-party costs order.
enrichment.ratio: Following Dymocks, a non-party director who initiates, controls and benefits from speculative litigation may be liable for all costs as the real party even without funding it; dishonest suppression of documents causing the litigation also provides sufficient causal connection.
legal_issues: Whether exceptional conduct is required for section 51(3) orders against directors
Whether lack of bona fide belief is necessary where the director is the real party
Causation between improper conduct and the costs sought
Application of Dymocks and Metalloy on real-party funding and control
linked_authorities: Dymocks Franchise Systems (NSW) Pty Ltd v Todd [2004] UKPC 39
Metalloy Supplies Ltd v MA (UK) Ltd [1997] 1 WLR 1613
Taylor v Pace Developments Ltd [1991] BCC 406

confidence.notes: Extensive fact findings, Dymocks analysis and dismissal on both exceptionality and causation are explicit.

notes: Estate agency commission appeal; exchange of contracts triggered 3% fee despite non-completion.

enrichment.short_title: Foxtons v Thesleff: commission payable on exchange not completion
key_facts: Foxtons were engaged on multiple agency terms at 3% commission to sell a London flat owned by the second defendant through her son as agent.
Foxtons introduced Mr Vafaian who exchanged contracts at £860,000 and paid a £86,000 deposit but failed to complete; the deposit was forfeited.
The property later sold for £843,000 through another agent.
Foxtons claimed commission on exchange; the defendants argued commission was payable only on completed sale.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against a county court decision dismissing Foxtons' claim for estate agency commission.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; commission of £30,315 inclusive of VAT plus interest awarded because fees became payable on exchange under clear multiple agency terms.
enrichment.ratio: Estate agents' commission is normally payable on completion but parties may agree otherwise; where terms state fees become payable upon exchange with a purchaser introduced by the agent, completion is not required and regulatory definitions do not override the contract.
legal_issues: Whether Foxtons' commission was payable on exchange or only on completion
Construction of 'purchaser' and 'achieved sale price' in agency terms
Whether 1991 Regulations definitions govern contractual meaning
Whether the first defendant agent was personally liable despite disclosed principal

confidence.notes: Contract terms, regulatory context and allowance of appeal with quantified judgment are clearly stated.
